> Then when they see the torment drawing near, the faces of the disbelievers will become gloomy, and it will be said ˹to them˺, “This is what you claimed would never come.”

**The Moment the Interval Ends**

The previous verse refused a date, and this one describes what happens when the date arrives. The transition is the whole answer to the demand for scheduling: the Book does not tell the mockers when the event will occur; it tells them what it will be like when it does. Knowing the hour in advance would have been information; being shown the scene is preparation. The sūrah gives the audience the second because the first was never theirs to have.

*When they see it close* — the phrase places the reader at the moment of the interval's collapse, which is the only vantage point from which the earlier mockery can be properly judged.

**Faces That Register the Verdict**

The Book uses the face as the register of a person's condition on the last day, and it does so with the confidence of a culture in which a face was a public document. In this verse the faces of the disbelievers turn dark — the Arabic carries the sense of a shadow falling across them, the expression of a man who has just been told something final in public. Elsewhere the Book reports that the condemned will be identifiable by their appearance and will be seized by their forelocks and feet (55:41), and that the guilty will be known by their marks. The body's testimony begins before any word is spoken.

Physical description of this kind is not decoration. It gives the audience something to imagine, and the sūrah's whole campaign has been to make a future event imaginable while there was still time to act on it.

**"This Is What You Claimed Would Never Come"**

The sentence spoken to them is a quotation of their own position, delivered at the moment it collapses. The Arabic puts the accusation in the second person, and the wording is a summary of everything the question in the earlier verse implied: the demand for a date, the conditional *if what you say is true*, and the years of confident dismissal. Nothing new is added to their record; the file is read back.

The Book records the same demand in its rawest form in the sūrah of the Spoils, where the Makkan leaders challenged God directly: *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.””* (8:32). The taunt is preserved, and the answer to it is this verse's scene. A demand for immediate proof is granted at the end of the interval, and the granting is not a vindication of the demanders.

**The Demand to Hasten the Punishment**

The Book reports that those who disbelieved were in the habit of asking for the punishment to be brought forward, and it treats the request as one of the proofs of their condition rather than as a theological question. A person who cannot wait for a verdict does not believe there is a verdict; a person who does believe it treats every delay as an opportunity. The sūrah has already made this point about the hidden hour in the context of testing, and the closing verses make it personal: the punishment will arrive, and the men who called for it early will not want it when they see it.

The pattern is not unique to this passage, and the Book answers it the same way each time. In Sūrah al-Ḥajj the demand is named outright: *“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise…”* (22:47). Sūrah Yūnus turns the request back on the one making it: *“Imagine if His torment were to overcome you by night or day—do the wicked realize what they are ˹really˺ asking Him to hasten?”* (10:50). A man who asks for the punishment to be moved forward is asking for the closing of his own record, and the Book reports the request as evidence against him rather than as a difficulty for the message.

**The Answer to a Demand for Evidence**

Behind the mockery in Makkah lay an argument about proof. The message claimed a coming day of judgement; the claim had not been verified; the audience offered to accept it the moment the punishment arrived. The Book's response is that the verification being requested is not a preliminary to faith; it is the end of the world as an arena of choice. An event that settles every question leaves nothing for belief to do, and the sūrah has said as much from its second verse onward, where human life was described as a test rather than as a demonstration.

**What the Believers Are Meant to Take From the Scene**

A community watching its tormentors from the street could be tempted toward two errors: to doubt the promise because of the delay, or to delight in the punishment prematurely. The verse avoids both by placing the scene where it belongs, in the hands of God and at the hour He has set. What the believers receive from the sentence is not satisfaction but orientation: the mockery that shapes their daily lives in the city has a shelf life, and the people producing it do not know what they will look like when it ends.

**Faces Across the Book's Descriptions of That Day**

The sūrah's portrait of darkened faces belongs to a set of images the Qur'an develops from sūrah to sūrah. In one passage the faces are divided into two parties and both are described: *“On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be bright, laughing and rejoicing, while ˹other˺ faces will be dusty, cast in gloom—”* (80:38–41). The dust on a face is not a metaphor for sadness; it is the condition of a person who has been dragged somewhere against his will. In another passage the humiliation is paired with a physical incapacity: *“˹Beware of˺ the Day the Shin ˹of Allah˺ will be bared, and the wicked will be asked to prostrate, but they will not be able to do so, with eyes downcast, totally covered with disgrace. For they were ˹always˺ called to prostrate ˹in the world˺ when they were fully capable ˹but they chose not to˺.”* (68:42–43).

Read together, the passages show what this verse's gloom amounts to. The faces of the disbelievers register a discovery that comes too late to act on, and the Book's description of that condition is drawn from the body because the body is what a person has been using to refuse.

**A Question for the Reader's Own Position**

The words are addressed to people who assumed the warning did not apply to them, and the sūrah has spent twenty-six verses establishing that everyone is addressed by it. The verse's function in the chapter's closing movement is to move the audience from argument to self-assessment. The question that follows in the next verse asks who among their protectors could save them; the answer must be given personally, by each hearer, and the sūrah leaves no formula by which someone else can give it on his behalf.
verses.28:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Consider this: whether Allah causes me and those with me to die or shows us mercy, who will save the disbelievers from a painful punishment?”

**A Question That Turns the Argument Around**

The mockers had been demanding to know when the threat would land on the believers. The answer they get does not tell them, and it moves the question to the other side of the table. Whatever happens to the Prophet ﷺ and his community — death or mercy — the party that needs rescuing is the party asking the questions. The commentators read the verse in exactly this way: the point is not the fate of the believers, which is settled either way, but the exposure of the men who thought the delay in punishing others was a guarantee about themselves.

The structure of the sentence is a trap with an open door. It grants the mockers their premise, imagines the worst outcome for the believers, and then asks the question that has no answer but one.

**"Whether He Causes Us to Die or Shows Us Mercy"**

Both outcomes are treated as acceptable, and the balance is worth noticing. The Book does not promise the believers safety, and this verse does not argue that the Prophet ﷺ would survive. The two possibilities named are death and mercy; both are delivered by the same hand, and neither is a defect in the mission. That composure is the foundation of everything the early community did under threat, and it kept them from converting the truth of their message into a claim about their own survival.

A message that needs its messenger alive to remain true is a fragile message. The verse deliberately detaches the two.

**A Community That Expected to Be Killed**

The Makkan believers had good reason to expect violence; the revelations they recited include instructions for patience under persecution, and the reports of the period describe torture and killing. This verse supplied a formulation that a person facing that prospect could carry: our end belongs to God, and the question of whether it comes early or late is not the test of anything. The Book uses the same reasoning elsewhere when it speaks of the two good outcomes awaiting those who fight in its path.

The argument is also an answer to a taunt. The mockers hinted that the Prophet's ﷺ death would prove the message false — a threat that has been aimed at missionaries in every century. The verse states that the argument was never about his lifespan.

**Who Could Save Them From the Punishment?**

The question in the second half of the verse has already been answered twice in this sūrah. The patrons of Makkah cannot deliver protection, as the earlier verse about the powerless helper established, and the Book states the general principle in a challenge to idolaters: *“Ask ˹them˺, “Consider then whatever ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah: if it was Allah's Will to harm me, could they undo that harm? Or if He willed ˹some˺ mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?” Say, “Allah is sufficient for me. In Him ˹alone˺ the faithful put their trust.””* (39:38). The logic is symmetrical, and the verse applies it to the party that assumed it was safe.

The Makkans had asked for a proof by punishment. The Book answers by naming the punishment and asking who would stand between them and it when it arrived.

**Why the Believers' Outcome Is Not the Argument**

A reader might expect the verse to promise the believers victory, and the omission is deliberate. The Book's case against the deniers is not that the Muslims will do well and the pagans badly; it is that the reckoning is God's, whatever happens in the interval. Had the verse promised survival and success, the faith of the community would have been tied to a political forecast, and its members would have been justified in measuring their confidence by events.

The Book avoids that arrangement in the Makkan period, when events looked hostile, and it lets the argument stand on the exposure of the deniers rather than on the prosperity of the believers.

The same question is put to the same audience in another sūrah, where the Book supplies the answer by naming the silence: *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet,˺ ‘Who can defend you by day or by night against the Most Compassionate?’ Still they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord.”* (21:42). The deniers are not being told that the believers' fate is uncertain; they are being asked who, among all that exists, would stand between them and the One they have angered. The question has no candidate on the list, and that absence is its force.

**The Rhetorical Force of the Word "Say"**

This verse is the second of four consecutive verses introduced by the command to speak, and the instruction is significant in a passage about mockery. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to be silent, to withdraw, or to retaliate; he is told to deliver a question. The community receives a line to speak in its own defence that does not depend on winning an argument and cannot be answered by the city's leaders. That is a strategy for a minority with no allies, and it is the strategy the sūrah ends with.

**The Avenues That Close on That Day**

The question in this verse has an answer that the Book states by elimination. The first avenue to close is intercession. The Book instructs the believers to spend before a day arrives when the arrangements of this world no longer function: *“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers.”* (2:254). The second avenue is ransom: *“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given.”* (2:48). Bargaining, friendship, and intercession are the three currencies of a tribal society, and all three are declared void.

What remains is stated positively elsewhere: *“Say, “All intercession belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. To Him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.””* (39:44). In a city where a man's protection was the protection his patrons could negotiate, the verse removes the negotiation and leaves the authority where the sūrah's first verse had placed it.

**What the Verse Leaves Behind**

A question that has only one possible answer functions as a statement, and this one leaves the audience with an exposure they must resolve. Every protector they trusted, every alliance they had purchased, and every arrangement of man and stone in the sanctuary are excluded by the same sentence. The Prophet ﷺ and his companions are handed over to God's decision about them; the mockers are handed over to a question they cannot answer, which is why the sūrah's remaining verses turn from argument to a declaration of faith.
verses.29:
> Say, “He is the Most Compassionate—in Him ˹alone˺ we believe, and in Him ˹alone˺ we trust. You will soon know who is clearly astray.”

**A Creed in One Sentence**

The verse is a declaration compressed into a single line: a name, a belief, and a reliance. The name is stated first because the sūrah has been building toward it from its third verse, where the flawless creation was attributed to the Most Compassionate, and from its nineteenth, where birds are held aloft by the same name. By the time the community is asked to announce its position, the audience has already been told what the name has done. What the verse adds is the community's response to it.

The order of the three elements matters. A name identifies; belief accepts the identification and all it implies; reliance acts on it. The verse moves a person from knowing to accepting to entrusting, in the space of a few words.

**Why the Name al-Raḥmān Carries the Argument**

The Most Compassionate is the name under which the works of the sūrah have been performed: the layered heavens, the lamps in the lowest of them, the earth made walkable, the water provided, the birds held in the air. Naming Him compassionately is the sūrah's way of saying that none of these arrangements is indifferent. The One who sustains is the One whose attribute is mercy, and the community's answer to a hostile city is to identify itself with that attribute.

The Makkans had heard the name before, and the Book records that it provoked dispute. Some of their objections concerned the name itself, and the new community's reply was not an argument about vocabulary but a public declaration that they belonged to the one it named.

**Tawakkul: Trust as Delegation, Not Passivity**

The verb *tawakkalnā* comes from a root meaning to rely on someone and to entrust an affair to him. The Qur'an defines the practice through the character of the one trusted rather than through a method: *“Say, “Allah is sufficient for me. In Him ˹alone˺ the faithful put their trust.””* (39:38). Reliance in this vocabulary is not the cancellation of effort but the transfer of the outcome — a man does what is his to do and does not treat the result as his own possession.

The verses of this sūrah have been setting up exactly that division of labour. The community cannot control its own safety, its own provision, or the date of the judgement, and it has been told so in four successive questions. What it can do is speak, work, and refuse to obey the men who block the road; the rest has been delegated, in this verse, on purpose.

**"You Will Soon Know Who Is Clearly Astray"**

The closing clause reverses the sentence the mockers had been using. In the earlier verse they asked their question with the proviso *if what you say is true*; here the community is told to announce that the verdict is coming and that the question is which party has been wandering. The Arabic puts the accusation in the vaguest possible form — *who* is clearly astray — and leaves the identification to the event, which is the sūrah's consistent method.

The phrase *clearly astray* repeats part of the deniers' own language from the earlier verse about the warner, where they said that the messenger was in obvious error. The sūrah sets the accusation and the answer in the same words and lets the Day decide.

**The Reading That Ends the Sentence Earlier**

The exegetes record a variant recitation of this verse. In the reading attributed to al-Kisāʾī, the last word is pronounced *sayaʿlamūn*, "they will soon know," which changes the scope of the sentence: what the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to say ends with the declaration of trust, and the announcement of coming knowledge becomes part of God's speech rather than part of the community's. The difference is small and the effect is instructive — in both readings the outcome is left to God, and the believers' line ends with the reliance they are told to profess.

**Faith and Reliance Held Together**

The verse pairs belief and trust, and the Qur'an almost never separates them for long. Belief without reliance remains a conclusion about the world; reliance without belief is a vague optimism. Together they produce the posture that the Makkan community needed: a settled conviction about who holds the affairs, plus a practical entrusting of their own affairs to Him. That posture is what allowed members of a powerless minority to speak in public about the future of their city.

**The Name That Opens a Sūrah**

The Most Compassionate is not only a name used in the middle of arguments; it is the opening of a sūrah devoted to the gifts by which creation is sustained: *“The Most Compassionate — taught the Quran, created humanity, ˹and˺ taught them speech.”* (55:1–4). The sūrah of the Most Compassionate then lists sign after sign, and its refrain asks which of the favours of the Lord the audience will deny. The placement in that sūrah matches the use made of the name here. Both passages attach the mercy in the name to something concrete: rain, fruit, guidance, and the ability to speak.

A community asked to announce its creed in public did so with a name that its opponents already disputed. It did not choose a slogan about victory or a claim about status; it chose the attribute under which its food arrived and its air stayed in place.

**The Confidence of the Closing Words**

The community is told to address a majority that could destroy it and to end its statement with a prediction. Everything about the arrangement is improbable except for the source of the prediction, and the verse rests its weight there. The sūrah's final question, still to come, will make the same move with a cup of water.
verses.30:
> Say, “Consider this: if your water were to sink ˹into the earth˺, then who ˹else˺ could bring you flowing water?”

**The Last Question Is the Most Ordinary One**

The sūrah that opened with the sovereignty of the One in whose hand authority rests closes with a glass of water. The movement from the first verse to the last is the chapter's own argument in miniature: authority over everything is exercised, in the end, in the daily details of a person's survival. The question is addressed to a city that drew its life from a spring and a scatter of wells, and it asks the inhabitants to imagine the ordinary infrastructure of their lives removed. Nothing in the sūrah's twenty-nine preceding verses is as concrete as this.

The choice of subject is also a statement about what counts as evidence. A merchant in Makkah did not need philosophy to know what water was worth; he had watched caravans ration it across the desert.

**The Water That Sinks Out of Reach**

The Arabic verb describes water going down into the earth and staying there — a sinking beyond the reach of wells, ropes, and hands. A spring does not run dry gradually in this image; it disappears into the ground, and the city is left standing above an aquifer it cannot touch. The Book states the same possibility elsewhere as a plain fact about divine control: *“We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth. And We are surely able to take it away.”* (23:18). The rain that soaks in is a gift; the rain that continues downward is a sentence.

**Who Could Bring It Back?**

The second half of the question has the same structure as the sūrah's other challenges. Every candidate is considered and excluded: not the gods of the sanctuary, not the tribal patrons, not the wealth of the merchants, not the engineering of any people in the region. The Book gives the same challenge to the Makkans in the sūrah of the Event about their food and their drink: *“Have you considered the water you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so? If We willed, We could make it salty. Will you not then give thanks?”* (56:68–70), and in the sūrah of the Frowning Face it directs people to consider the whole chain of their meals, from rainfall to grain and fruit (80:24–30).

Water is chosen for the last of these arguments because no one can claim credit for it and no one can replace it.

**Water as the Measure of Provision**

The Book treats water as the clearest image of provision in general, and it recurs in that role: rain sent down to give life to a dead land and to provide for every creature in it (25:48–49); the earth stirred to life by rain and brought back from lifelessness (41:39); every living thing created from water (21:30); the earth made habitable and the sky turned into a canopy over it (2:22). Each of these passages makes the same argument in a different register: the ordinary gift is the one that is never counted until it is gone.

The Makkans of the sūrah's audience were the heirs of a sanctuary built around a well. Their city existed because water was there, and their history included a miracle of water in the desert that they told about their own origins.

**Flowing Water and the Word Behind It**

The adjective rendered *flowing* is *maʿīn*, which describes water that runs and shows itself — the opposite of water standing still, hidden, or brackish. The commentators record two explanations of the word: some connected it with the eye, since flowing water is water that one can see, and others with the verb for running. Either way the contrast with the imagined disaster is exact. What sinks into the earth is invisible and unreachable; what is asked for is water that appears and moves where people can reach it.

The choice of word closes the verse's argument. Even if someone could find the vanished water, bringing it back to where it could be used is a second act of creation.

**A Question Every Generation Has to Answer**

The first audience was asked about their wells; later generations of Muslims would be asked about their reservoirs, pipelines, and desalination plants, and the answer does not change with the technology. A city can build machines to lift water and then discover that the rain feeding the aquifer has stopped. The Book's argument is not against engineering but against the assumption that the chain of causes begins with human beings.

The question is phrased as a challenge to name a candidate, which is the same form the sūrah has used from its opening verse. The reader is left with the list of possible suppliers and no answer to give.

**The Same Water Can Bring the Garden or End It**

Two other passages complete the argument. In one, a garden reaches its fullest beauty and the owners conclude that they control what happens to it: *“Then just as the earth looks its best, perfectly beautified, and its people think they have full control over it, there comes to it Our command by night or by day, so We mow it down as if it never flourished yesterday!”* (10:24). The Book's image of the owners' mistake is not the neglect of their land; it is their confidence in it. In another passage, rain produces crops of every colour, and then the same crops dry, wither, and are reduced to chaff (39:21). The water given to the garden is the same water that makes the harvest possible, and its withdrawal leaves both the harvest and the confidence gone.

A city fed by a spring was being asked to see itself in both pictures: prosperous for as long as the flow continued, and unable to produce a single day of that flow by itself.

**The Design of the Chapter, Complete**

The thirty verses have travelled from an assertion of sovereignty, through creation and testing, judgement and knowledge, provision and protection, to this final question about a cup of water. Each earlier argument has been leading to the point where the most basic necessity is placed in the same hand as the sovereignty that began the chapter. A reader who closes the sūrah has been shown that the authority of the first verse is present in the last one, and that the test which the second verse described is conducted with water, bread, hearing, sight, and time — all of them gifts, none of them owned.
